Reference: Caliendo and Parro (2015)

Model Setting

The paper builds sectoral linkages, trade in intermediate goods and sectoral heterogeneity in production into the Ricardian model of Eaton and Kortum (2002) in order to quantify the trade and welfare effects of tariff changes, and applies it to the tariff reductions of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) between Mexico, Canada and the U.S. The motivation is that sectors and countries are interrelated. A tariff cut in one sector lowers prices in that sector, in the sectors that buy materials from it, and in non-tradable sectors that use tradable inputs, and non-tradables are most of final demand (more than 80 percent in the U.S. in 1993). Three facts make this important for NAFTA. Tariffs were heterogeneous across sectors: in 1993 the average sectoral tariffs applied to NAFTA partners were 12.5 percent (Mexico), 4.2 percent (Canada) and 2.7 percent (U.S.). Most trade is in intermediate goods: 82.1, 72.3 and 72.8 percent of the imports of Mexico, Canada and the U.S. from NAFTA partners. And input-output (I-O) tables show that sectors buy most inputs from other sectors (the mean own-sector share is 16 percent in the U.S. and 13 percent in Mexico), with tradables supplying 23 to 32 percent of the inputs of non-tradables and non-tradables 26 to 34 percent of the inputs of tradables.

The paper makes three contributions. First, a tractable multi-country, multi-sector model with tradable and non-tradable sectors linked through an I-O structure, which is solved in relative changes (the hat algebra of Dekle, Eaton and Kortum 2008) and reduces to one equation per country; the only parameters to estimate are the sectoral trade elasticities. Second, a new estimator of these elasticities that uses a triple ratio of bilateral trade flows and tariffs, needs no symmetry of trade costs and no data on domestic sales, and is valid in any model with a multiplicative gravity equation. Third, a quantification with 31 countries and 40 sectors calibrated to 1993. NAFTA's tariff reductions raise welfare by 1.31 percent in Mexico and 0.08 percent in the U.S. and lower it by 0.06 percent in Canada; intra-bloc trade rises by 118 percent for Mexico, 11 percent for Canada and 41 percent for the U.S. Welfare and trade effects are much smaller in models without sectoral heterogeneity, intermediate goods or I-O linkages.

Households and Intermediate Goods Producers

There are NNN countries, indexed by iii and nnn, and JJJ sectors, indexed by jjj and kkk. Sectors are tradable or non-tradable. Labour is the only factor; it is mobile across sectors and immobile across countries, and all markets are perfectly competitive. In country nnn a measure LnL_nLn​ of representative households consume final goods CnjC^j_nCnj​ with Cobb-Douglas preferences:

u(Cn)=∏j=1J(Cnj)αnj,∑j=1Jαnj=1(1)u(C_n)=\prod_{j=1}^J\left(C^j_n\right)^{\alpha^j_n},\qquad\sum_{j=1}^J\alpha^j_n=1 \tag{1}u(Cn​)=j=1∏J​(Cnj​)αnj​,j=1∑J​αnj​=1(1)

Household income InI_nIn​ consists of labour income at wage wnw_nwn​ and lump-sum transfers (tariff revenue and transfers from the rest of the world). In each sector jjj a continuum of intermediate goods ωj∈[0,1]\omega^j\in[0,1]ωj∈[0,1] is produced with labour and composite intermediate goods (materials) from all sectors:

qnj(ωj)=znj(ωj)[lnj(ωj)]γnj∏k=1J[mnk,j(ωj)]γnk,j(2)q^j_n(\omega^j)=z^j_n(\omega^j)\left[l^j_n(\omega^j)\right]^{\gamma^j_n}\prod_{k=1}^J\left[m^{k,j}_n(\omega^j)\right]^{\gamma^{k,j}_n} \tag{2}qnj​(ωj)=znj​(ωj)[lnj​(ωj)]γnj​k=1∏J​[mnk,j​(ωj)]γnk,j​(2)

where znj(ωj)z^j_n(\omega^j)znj​(ωj) is the efficiency of producing ωj\omega^jωj in country nnn, lnj(ωj)l^j_n(\omega^j)lnj​(ωj) is labour, mnk,j(ωj)m^{k,j}_n(\omega^j)mnk,j​(ωj) is the quantity of the composite good of sector kkk used as material, γnk,j≥0\gamma^{k,j}_n\geq0γnk,j​≥0 is the share of materials from sector kkk in the production of sector jjj, and γnj≥0\gamma^j_n\geq0γnj​≥0 is the share of value added, with ∑k=1Jγnk,j=1−γnj\sum_{k=1}^J\gamma^{k,j}_n=1-\gamma^j_n∑k=1J​γnk,j​=1−γnj​. Both sets of shares vary across countries and sectors. With constant returns and perfect competition, firms price at unit cost cnj/znj(ωj)c^j_n/z^j_n(\omega^j)cnj​/znj​(ωj), where the cost of an input bundle is:

cnj=Υnjwnγnj∏k=1J(Pnk)γnk,j(3)c^j_n=\Upsilon^j_nw_n^{\gamma^j_n}\prod_{k=1}^J\left(P^k_n\right)^{\gamma^{k,j}_n} \tag{3}cnj​=Υnj​wnγnj​​k=1∏J​(Pnk​)γnk,j​(3)

Here PnkP^k_nPnk​ is the price of the composite intermediate good of sector kkk and Υnj\Upsilon^j_nΥnj​ is a constant that depends only on the shares. This equation is the key difference from a one-sector model or a multi-sector model without linkages: the cost of the input bundle depends on wages and on the prices of all composite goods, tradable and non-tradable, so a policy that changes the price in one sector affects every sector indirectly.

Composite Intermediate Goods and Trade Costs

Producers of the composite intermediate good in sector jjj of country nnn supply QnjQ^j_nQnj​ at minimum cost, buying each ωj\omega^jωj from the lowest-cost supplier in the world:

Qnj=[∫rnj(ωj)1−1/σjdωj]σj/(σj−1)(4)Q^j_n=\left[\int r^j_n(\omega^j)^{1-1/\sigma^j}d\omega^j\right]^{\sigma^j/(\sigma^j-1)} \tag{4}Qnj​=[∫rnj​(ωj)1−1/σjdωj]σj/(σj−1)(4)

where σj>0\sigma^j>0σj>0 is the elasticity of substitution across intermediate goods within sector jjj and rnj(ωj)r^j_n(\omega^j)rnj​(ωj) is the demand for ωj\omega^jωj from the lowest-cost supplier. Demand is rnj(ωj)=(pnj(ωj)/Pnj)−σjQnjr^j_n(\omega^j)=\left(p^j_n(\omega^j)/P^j_n\right)^{-\sigma^j}Q^j_nrnj​(ωj)=(pnj​(ωj)/Pnj​)−σjQnj​, where pnj(ωj)p^j_n(\omega^j)pnj​(ωj) is the lowest price of ωj\omega^jωj in country nnn and PnjP^j_nPnj​ is the unit price of the composite good, the usual constant elasticity price index over pnj(ωj)p^j_n(\omega^j)pnj​(ωj). The composite good of sector jjj is used as material in all sectors kkk, in the amounts mnj,k(ωk)m^{j,k}_n(\omega^k)mnj,k​(ωk), and as the final good CnjC^j_nCnj​. Searching for the lowest-cost supplier is what separates the model from Armington models: the set of goods sourced from each country is endogenous, so tariff changes operate on the extensive margin.

Trade is subject to iceberg costs and ad-valorem tariffs. Shipping one unit of a tradable sector jjj good from country iii to country nnn requires producing dnij≥1d^j_{ni}\geq1dnij​≥1 units in iii, with dnnj=1d^j_{nn}=1dnnj​=1, and imports of nnn from iii pay a tariff τnij\tau^j_{ni}τnij​ on unit prices. and the triangle inequality κnhjκhij≥κnij\kappa^j_{nh}\kappa^j_{hi}\geq\kappa^j_{ni}κnhj​κhij​≥κnij​ is assumed for all n,h,in,h,in,h,i. A unit of ωj\omega^jωj produced in iii is available in nnn at cijκnij/zij(ωj)c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni}/z^j_i(\omega^j)cij​κnij​/zij​(ωj), so:

pnj(ωj)=min⁡i{cijκnijzij(ωj)}(6)p^j_n(\omega^j)=\min_i\left\{\frac{c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni}}{z^j_i(\omega^j)}\right\} \tag{6}pnj​(ωj)=imin​{zij​(ωj)cij​κnij​​}(6)

Technology, Prices and Expenditure Shares

Following Eaton and Kortum (2002), the efficiency of producing ωj\omega^jωj in country nnn is a draw from a Frechet distribution:

Fnj(z)=e−λnjz−θj(7)F^j_n(z)=e^{-\lambda^j_nz^{-\theta^j}} \tag{7}Fnj​(z)=e−λnj​z−θj(7)

The location parameter λnj≥0\lambda^j_n\geq0λnj​≥0 varies by country and sector; a higher λnj\lambda^j_nλnj​ raises average productivity (absolute advantage). The shape parameter θj\theta^jθj varies by sector; a smaller θj\theta^jθj means more dispersion of productivity across goods (comparative advantage). Draws are independent across goods, sectors and countries, and 1+θj>σj1+\theta^j>\sigma^j1+θj>σj. The price of a good offered by iii in nnn is then Frechet, the lowest price in nnn is distributed with parameter Φnj=∑i=1Nλij(cijκnij)−θj\Phi^j_n=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda^j_i(c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni})^{-\theta^j}Φnj​=∑i=1N​λij​(cij​κnij​)−θj, and integrating gives the price of the composite good:

Pnj=Aj[∑i=1Nλij(cijκnij)−θj]−1/θj(8)P^j_n=A^j\left[\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda^j_i\left(c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni}\right)^{-\theta^j}\right]^{-1/\theta^j} \tag{8}Pnj​=Aj[i=1∑N​λij​(cij​κnij​)−θj]−1/θj(8)

where AjA^jAj is a constant (a Gamma function of θj\theta^jθj and σj\sigma^jσj). In a non-tradable sector the same formula collapses to Pnj=Aj(λnj)−1/θjcnjP^j_n=A^j(\lambda^j_n)^{-1/\theta^j}c^j_nPnj​=Aj(λnj​)−1/θjcnj​. The statistic Φnj\Phi^j_nΦnj​ summarizes world technologies, input costs, geography and tariffs; unlike in Eaton and Kortum (2002) it is sector specific and correlated across sectors through the shares γnk,j\gamma^{k,j}_nγnk,j​. The consumption price index is:

Pn=∏j=1J(Pnj/αnj)αnj(9)P_n=\prod_{j=1}^J\left(P^j_n/\alpha^j_n\right)^{\alpha^j_n} \tag{9}Pn​=j=1∏J​(Pnj​/αnj​)αnj​(9)

πnij=λij[cijκnij]−θj∑h=1Nλhj[chjκnhj]−θj(10)\pi^j_{ni}=\frac{\lambda^j_i\left[c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni}\right]^{-\theta^j}}{\sum_{h=1}^N\lambda^j_h\left[c^j_h\kappa^j_{nh}\right]^{-\theta^j}} \tag{10}πnij​=∑h=1N​λhj​[chj​κnhj​]−θjλij​[cij​κnij​]−θj​(10)

Real Wages: the Role of Intermediates and Linkages

Solving the first and third conditions for w^n/P^nj\hat{w}_n/\hat{P}^j_nw^n​/P^nj​ with i=ni=ni=n (where κ^nnj=1\hat{\kappa}^j_{nn}=1κ^nnj​=1) and aggregating across sectors with weights αnj\alpha^j_nαnj​ gives the change in the real wage:

ln⁡w^nP^n=−∑j=1Jαnjθjln⁡π^nnj⏟Final goods−∑j=1Jαnjθj1−γnjγnjln⁡π^nnj⏟Intermediate goods−∑j=1Jαnjγnjln⁡∏k=1J(P^nk/P^nj)γnk,j⏟Sectoral linkages(21)\ln\frac{\hat{w}_n}{\hat{P}_n}=-\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^J\frac{\alpha^j_n}{\theta^j}\ln\hat{\pi}^j_{nn}}_{\text{Final goods}}-\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^J\frac{\alpha^j_n}{\theta^j}\frac{1-\gamma^j_n}{\gamma^j_n}\ln\hat{\pi}^j_{nn}}_{\text{Intermediate goods}}-\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^J\frac{\alpha^j_n}{\gamma^j_n}\ln\prod_{k=1}^J\left(\hat{P}^k_n/\hat{P}^j_n\right)^{\gamma^{k,j}_n}}_{\text{Sectoral linkages}} \tag{21}lnP^n​w^n​​=−Final goodsj=1∑J​θjαnj​​lnπ^nnj​​​−Intermediate goodsj=1∑J​θjαnj​​γnj​1−γnj​​lnπ^nnj​​​−Sectoral linkagesj=1∑J​γnj​αnj​​lnk=1∏J​(P^nk​/P^nj​)γnk,j​​​(21)

where P^n\hat{P}_nP^n​ is the change in the consumption price index. All general equilibrium effects on real wages are summarized by the changes in the domestic expenditure shares π^nnj\hat{\pi}^j_{nn}π^nnj​ and in sectoral prices P^nj\hat{P}^j_nP^nj​, and each term adds an effect relative to a benchmark. If γnj=1\gamma^j_n=1γnj​=1 for all jjj, goods are produced with labour only and only the first term remains: the multi-sector version of the formula of Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare (2012), in which the more negatively correlated αnj/θj\alpha^j_n/\theta^jαnj​/θj is with π^nnj\hat{\pi}^j_{nn}π^nnj​, the larger the gain, so that heterogeneity in θj\theta^jθj matters. If γnj≠1\gamma^j_n\neq1γnj​=1 and γnj,j=1−γnj\gamma^{j,j}_n=1-\gamma^j_nγnj,j​=1−γnj​, materials come only from the own sector: cheaper tradable intermediates lower the cost of producers who use them, which adds the second term. In the general model the third term captures the I-O structure: the larger γnk,j\gamma^{k,j}_nγnk,j​ for sectors kkk whose prices fall more, the larger the fall in the material cost of sector jjj. The term resembles a geometric weighted average of changes in material prices and vanishes only under substantial symmetry. Real wages are not welfare when tariff revenue is rebated: with η=wnLn/In\eta=w_nL_n/I_nη=wn​Ln​/In​, the paper states I^n/P^n=ηw^n/P^n+(1−η)R^n/P^n\hat{I}_n/\hat{P}_n=\eta\hat{w}_n/\hat{P}_n+(1-\eta)\hat{R}_n/\hat{P}_nI^n​/P^n​=ηw^n​/P^n​+(1−η)R^n​/P^n​.

Welfare: Terms of Trade and Volume of Trade

Welfare of the representative consumer is Wn=In/PnW_n=I_n/P_nWn​=In​/Pn​. Totally differentiating, holding deficits and iceberg costs fixed, the paper obtains:

dln⁡Wn=1In∑j=1J∑i=1N(Enijdln⁡cnj−Mnijdln⁡cij)⏟Terms of trade+1In∑j=1J∑i=1NτnijMnij(dln⁡Mnij−dln⁡cij)⏟Volume of trade(22)d\ln W_n=\frac{1}{I_n}\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^N\left(E^j_{ni}d\ln c^j_n-M^j_{ni}d\ln c^j_i\right)}_{\text{Terms of trade}}+\frac{1}{I_n}\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^N\tau^j_{ni}M^j_{ni}\left(d\ln M^j_{ni}-d\ln c^j_i\right)}_{\text{Volume of trade}} \tag{22}dlnWn​=In​1​Terms of tradej=1∑J​i=1∑N​(Enij​dlncnj​−Mnij​dlncij​)​​+In​1​Volume of tradej=1∑J​i=1∑N​τnij​Mnij​(dlnMnij​−dlncij​)​​(22)

The first term is the multilateral and multi-sectoral terms of trade effect and the second the volume of trade effect. The derivation writes dln⁡Wn=(wnLn/In)dln⁡wn+(Rn/In)dln⁡Rn−dln⁡Pnd\ln W_n=(w_nL_n/I_n)d\ln w_n+(R_n/I_n)d\ln R_n-d\ln P_ndlnWn​=(wn​Ln​/In​)dlnwn​+(Rn​/In​)dlnRn​−dlnPn​, differentiates tariff revenue, uses dln⁡Pnj=∑i=1Nπnij(dln⁡cij+dln⁡τ~nij)d\ln P^j_n=\sum_{i=1}^N\pi^j_{ni}(d\ln c^j_i+d\ln\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni})dlnPnj​=∑i=1N​πnij​(dlncij​+dlnτ~nij​) from the price index, replaces αnj\alpha^j_nαnj​ with the expenditure equation, and eliminates the wage with the input cost equation. The direct effect of tariffs on consumer prices cancels against the rebated revenue, so tariffs matter only through world prices and through quantities. Conditional on exporting, the world price of a good that nnn sells to iii is cnjdnij/znj(ωj)c^j_nd^j_{ni}/z^j_n(\omega^j)cnj​dnij​/znj​(ωj), so changes in input costs measure changes in trade prices. The terms of trade effect is a weighted change of export prices relative to import prices, with bilateral sectoral exports and imports as weights. A sector's contribution cannot be signed in general; a sufficient condition for a positive contribution is that the sector is a net exporter and its export price rises relative to its import price. Sectoral variation matters here only because of intermediates: if γnj=1\gamma^j_n=1γnj​=1 then cnj=wnc^j_n=w_ncnj​=wn​ and the term collapses to ∑i=1NMni(dln⁡wn−dln⁡wi)\sum_{i=1}^NM_{ni}(d\ln w_n-d\ln w_i)∑i=1N​Mni​(dlnwn​−dlnwi​), with MniM_{ni}Mni​ total imports of nnn from iii, exactly as in a one-sector model. The volume of trade effect is the change in import volumes (import values deflated by import prices) weighted by initial tariffs: an import carries a wedge τnij\tau^j_{ni}τnij​ between its value to the importer and its world price, so trade created across a positive tariff raises welfare and trade diverted from a tariff-ridden source lowers it. The same objects define bilateral measures of the change in terms of trade and in the volume of trade between nnn and iii:

dln⁡totni=∑j=1J(Enijdln⁡cnj−Mnijdln⁡cij)(23)d\ln tot_{ni}=\sum_{j=1}^J\left(E^j_{ni}d\ln c^j_n-M^j_{ni}d\ln c^j_i\right) \tag{23}dlntotni​=j=1∑J​(Enij​dlncnj​−Mnij​dlncij​)(23)
dln⁡votni=∑j=1JτnijMnij(dln⁡Mnij−dln⁡cij)(24)d\ln vot_{ni}=\sum_{j=1}^J\tau^j_{ni}M^j_{ni}\left(d\ln M^j_{ni}-d\ln c^j_i\right) \tag{24}dlnvotni​=j=1∑J​τnij​Mnij​(dlnMnij​−dlncij​)(24)

The sectoral measures dln⁡totnjd\ln tot^j_ndlntotnj​ and dln⁡votnjd\ln vot^j_ndlnvotnj​ are defined by the same two expressions with the sum taken over partners i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,Ni=1,…,N for a given sector jjj instead of over sectors. It follows that dln⁡Wn=1In∑i=1N(dln⁡totni+dln⁡votni)=1In∑j=1J(dln⁡totnj+dln⁡votnj)d\ln W_n=\frac{1}{I_n}\sum_{i=1}^N(d\ln tot_{ni}+d\ln vot_{ni})=\frac{1}{I_n}\sum_{j=1}^J(d\ln tot^j_n+d\ln vot^j_n)dlnWn​=In​1​∑i=1N​(dlntotni​+dlnvotni​)=In​1​∑j=1J​(dlntotnj​+dlnvotnj​).

Taking the Model to the Data and Solution Algorithm

The data needed are bilateral trade flows MnijM^j_{ni}Mnij​, value added VnjV^j_nVnj​, gross production YnjY^j_nYnj​ and I-O tables. Domestic sales are Mnnj=Ynj−∑i=1,i≠nNMinjM^j_{nn}=Y^j_n-\sum_{i=1,i\neq n}^NM^j_{in}Mnnj​=Ynj​−∑i=1,i=nN​Minj​, expenditure is Xnij=Mnij(1+τnij)X^j_{ni}=M^j_{ni}(1+\tau^j_{ni})Xnij​=Mnij​(1+τnij​), and πnij=Xnij/∑i=1NXnij\pi^j_{ni}=X^j_{ni}/\sum_{i=1}^NX^j_{ni}πnij​=Xnij​/∑i=1N​Xnij​. The value added share is γnj=Vnj/Ynj\gamma^j_n=V^j_n/Y^j_nγnj​=Vnj​/Ynj​, and γnj,k\gamma^{j,k}_nγnj,k​ is the share of sector jjj in the intermediate consumption of sector kkk times 1−γnk1-\gamma^k_n1−γnk​. Final consumption shares are residual:

αnj=Ynj+Dnj−∑k=1Jγnj,kYnkIn(25)\alpha^j_n=\frac{Y^j_n+D^j_n-\sum_{k=1}^J\gamma^{j,k}_nY^k_n}{I_n} \tag{25}αnj​=In​Ynj​+Dnj​−∑k=1J​γnj,k​Ynk​​(25)

The algorithm starts from a guess of the wage changes w^=(w^1,…,w^N)\hat{\mathbf{w}}=(\hat{w}_1,\ldots,\hat{w}_N)w^=(w^1​,…,w^N​). Given w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^, the input cost and price index conditions are J×NJ\times NJ×N equations in J×NJ\times NJ×N prices and give P^nj(w^)\hat{P}^j_n(\hat{\mathbf{w}})P^nj​(w^) and c^nj(w^)\hat{c}^j_n(\hat{\mathbf{w}})c^nj​(w^); the trade share condition gives πnij′(w^)\pi^{j'}_{ni}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})πnij′​(w^). The expenditure condition is then linear in the vector X\mathbf{X}X of the JNJNJN counterfactual expenditures:

Ω(w^)X=Δ(w^),Ω(w^)=I−F(w^)−H~(w^)(26)\mathbf{\Omega}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})\mathbf{X}=\Delta(\hat{\mathbf{w}}),\qquad\mathbf{\Omega}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})=I-\mathcal{F}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})-\tilde{H}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}) \tag{26}Ω(w^)X=Δ(w^),Ω(w^)=I−F(w^)−H~(w^)(26)

where Δ(w^)\Delta(\hat{\mathbf{w}})Δ(w^) stacks αnj(w^nwnLn+Dn′)\alpha^j_n(\hat{w}_nw_nL_n+D'_n)αnj​(w^n​wn​Ln​+Dn′​), the matrix F(w^)\mathcal{F}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})F(w^) collects the tariff revenue terms (built from αnj\alpha^j_nαnj​ and 1−Fnj′1-F^{j'}_n1−Fnj′​ with Fnj′=∑i=1Nπnij′/(1+τnij′)F^{j'}_n=\sum_{i=1}^N\pi^{j'}_{ni}/(1+\tau^{j'}_{ni})Fnj′​=∑i=1N​πnij′​/(1+τnij′​)), and H~(w^)\tilde{H}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})H~(w^) collects the I-O terms γnj,kπink′/(1+τink′)\gamma^{j,k}_n\pi^{k'}_{in}/(1+\tau^{k'}_{in})γnj,k​πink′​/(1+τink′​). Inverting gives X(w^)=Ω−1(w^)Δ(w^)\mathbf{X}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})=\mathbf{\Omega}^{-1}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})\Delta(\hat{\mathbf{w}})X(w^)=Ω−1(w^)Δ(w^). Substituting into the trade balance condition leaves NNN equations (one trade balance per country) in NNN unknown wage changes, and the guess is adjusted until they hold. The matrix Ω\mathbf{\Omega}Ω is where the model differs from simpler ones: if γnj,j=1−γnj\gamma^{j,j}_n=1-\gamma^j_nγnj,j​=1−γnj​, expenditures of each country can be solved independently of those of other countries, and with one sector Ω\mathbf{\Omega}Ω collapses to a scalar as in Alvarez and Lucas (2007).

Estimating Sectoral Trade Elasticities

The parameter θj\theta^jθj governs how trade shares respond to tariffs. With a large θj\theta^jθj (little dispersion) goods are close substitutes across suppliers and small tariff changes move trade a lot through the extensive margin. Take three countries nnn, iii and hhh and the product of sector jjj flows in one direction around the triangle divided by the product in the other direction. By the expenditure share equation:

XnijXihjXhnjXnhjXhijXinj=(κnijκinjκihjκhijκhnjκnhj)−θj(27)\frac{X^j_{ni}X^j_{ih}X^j_{hn}}{X^j_{nh}X^j_{hi}X^j_{in}}=\left(\frac{\kappa^j_{ni}}{\kappa^j_{in}}\frac{\kappa^j_{ih}}{\kappa^j_{hi}}\frac{\kappa^j_{hn}}{\kappa^j_{nh}}\right)^{-\theta^j} \tag{27}Xnhj​Xhij​Xinj​Xnij​Xihj​Xhnj​​=(κinj​κnij​​κhij​κihj​​κnhj​κhnj​​)−θj(27)

Total expenditures, technologies, input costs and price indices all cancel, because each country appears once as importer and once as exporter in the numerator and in the denominator. Trade costs are allowed to be asymmetric:

ln⁡κnij=ln⁡τ~nij+ln⁡dnij=ln⁡τ~nij+νnij+μnj+δij+εnij(28)\ln\kappa^j_{ni}=\ln\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni}+\ln d^j_{ni}=\ln\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni}+\nu^j_{ni}+\mu^j_n+\delta^j_i+\varepsilon^j_{ni} \tag{28}lnκnij​=lnτ~nij​+lndnij​=lnτ~nij​+νnij​+μnj​+δij​+εnij​(28)

where νnij=νinj\nu^j_{ni}=\nu^j_{in}νnij​=νinj​ captures symmetric bilateral costs (distance, language, common border, belonging to a free trade area), μnj\mu^j_nμnj​ is an importer sectoral fixed effect and δij\delta^j_iδij​ an exporter sectoral fixed effect (for example non-tariff barriers), and εnij\varepsilon^j_{ni}εnij​ is a random deviation from symmetry assumed orthogonal to tariffs. Substituting into the triple ratio:

ln⁡(XnijXihjXhnjXinjXhijXnhj)=−θjln⁡(τ~nijτ~injτ~ihjτ~hijτ~hnjτ~nhj)+ε~j(29)\ln\left(\frac{X^j_{ni}X^j_{ih}X^j_{hn}}{X^j_{in}X^j_{hi}X^j_{nh}}\right)=-\theta^j\ln\left(\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{in}}\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{ih}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{hi}}\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{hn}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{nh}}\right)+\tilde{\varepsilon}^j \tag{29}ln(Xinj​Xhij​Xnhj​Xnij​Xihj​Xhnj​​)=−θjln(τ~inj​τ~nij​​τ~hij​τ~ihj​​τ~nhj​τ~hnj​​)+ε~j(29)

where ε~j=εinj−εnij+εhij−εihj+εnhj−εhnj\tilde{\varepsilon}^j=\varepsilon^j_{in}-\varepsilon^j_{ni}+\varepsilon^j_{hi}-\varepsilon^j_{ih}+\varepsilon^j_{nh}-\varepsilon^j_{hn}ε~j=εinj​−εnij​+εhij​−εihj​+εnhj​−εhnj​. The symmetric components and both sets of fixed effects cancel, so θj\theta^jθj is identified from the cross-sectional covariation of asymmetries in trade flows with asymmetries in tariffs; the only restriction is that ε~j\tilde{\varepsilon}^jε~j is orthogonal to tariffs. Relative to the odds ratio of Head and Ries (2001) and to tetrad methods, the estimator does not assume symmetric trade costs, does not use domestic sales (which combine production and trade data), uses three countries instead of four, and needs no reference country. It remains subject to the concern that trade policy is endogenous. Estimation is by ordinary least squares sector by sector on 1993 data, dropping zeros, for 16 economies (Brazil is dropped because of its currency crisis, Mexico is excluded, and triples that involve both Canada and the U.S. are removed); there are 9138 observations over the 20 tradable sectors.

  • Estimates: all coefficients have the expected sign in the full sample and range from 0.37 (Other Transport) to 51.08 (Petroleum); equality across sectors is rejected (F(17,7294)=7.52F(17,7294)=7.52F(17,7294)=7.52). The aggregate elasticity is 4.55 with standard error 0.35.

  • Benchmark values: the calibration uses the 99 percent sample, which drops in each sector the countries with the smallest 1 percent of trade. Values include 9.11 for Agriculture, 13.53 for Mining, 2.62 for Food, 8.10 for Textile, 64.85 for Petroleum, 3.13 for Chemicals, 12.95 for Office, 12.91 for Electrical and 3.95 for Communication; the aggregate is 4.49.

  • Robustness: Basic metals, Machinery n.e.c. and Auto change sign in the 97.5 percent sample and are replaced by the mean manufacturing estimate. Adding importer and exporter fixed effects is a further check.

Data and Counterfactual Design

The base year is 1993, the year before NAFTA. The sample has N=31N=31N=31 (30 countries and a constructed rest of the world) and J=40J=40J=40 sectors at the two-digit ISIC Rev. 3 level, 20 tradable (agriculture, mining and 18 manufacturing sectors) and 20 non-tradable. Bilateral trade comes from COMTRADE, gross output and value added from OECD STAN, INDSTAT2 and the OECD Input-Output database, I-O tables from the World Input-Output Database and the OECD, and effectively applied tariffs for 1993 and 2005 from UNCTAD-TRAINS. Because aggregate deficits are exogenous, the model is first calibrated with the observed deficits and then solved with Dn′=0D'_n=0Dn′​=0; this no-deficit economy is the base for the results below. The alternative of holding deficits constant as a share of world GDP gives similar welfare effects (1.17, −0.04-0.04−0.04 and 0.09 percent for Mexico, Canada and the U.S.). Two counterfactuals are run. The first changes tariffs among NAFTA members from their 1993 to their 2005 levels and keeps all other tariffs at 1993 levels. The second compares the observed change in world tariffs between 1993 and 2005 with the same change holding NAFTA tariffs at 1993 levels. Technology and other trade costs are held fixed throughout, so the results are the effects of tariff reductions only and not of the whole agreement.

Results

  • Welfare: Mexico gains 1.31 percent (terms of trade −0.41-0.41−0.41, volume of trade 1.72), Canada loses 0.06 percent (−0.11-0.11−0.11 and 0.04) and the U.S. gains 0.08 percent (0.04 and 0.04). Real wages rise in all three countries, by 1.72, 0.32 and 0.11 percent.

  • Trade creation and diversion: the volume of trade effect with NAFTA partners is 1.80, 0.08 and 0.04 percent for Mexico, Canada and the U.S., and with the rest of the world −0.08-0.08−0.08, −0.04-0.04−0.04 and 0.00 percent. Trade created inside the bloc is much larger than trade diverted from outside.

  • Terms of trade: export prices fall on average by 2 percent in Mexico and 0.6 percent in Canada and rise by 0.1 percent in the U.S., because cheaper materials outweigh higher wages in the first two. The bilateral terms of trade with NAFTA partners change by −0.39-0.39−0.39, −0.09-0.09−0.09 and 0.03 percent.

  • Sectors: Electrical Machinery, Communication Equipment and Auto account for 76 percent of Mexico's terms of trade deterioration and 51 percent of the U.S. improvement. Mexico's 1993 tariffs on them were 13.4, 14.9 and 15.5 percent, their material shares are 82, 82 and 73 percent (against an average of 49), and they are tightly linked. Textiles (the most protected sector in Mexico, about 18 percent), Petroleum (the highest elasticity) and Electrical Machinery account for more than half of the volume of trade effect in Mexico and the U.S.

  • Trade: Mexico's imports from Canada and the U.S. rise by 116.60 and 118.31 percent, Canada's imports from Mexico and the U.S. by 58.57 and 9.49 percent, and U.S. imports from Mexico and Canada by 109.54 and 6.57 percent. Mexico becomes more specialized: the share of Electrical Machinery in its exports rises from 20.79 to 34.07 percent and its normalized Herfindahl index from 0.092 to 0.138, while the index falls from 0.083 to 0.081 in Canada and from 0.042 to 0.040 in the U.S.

  • Rest of the world: effects are small; the largest losses are about 0.03 percent, for China and Korea.

  • World tariff changes: with all observed tariff changes every country gains; China gains 13.9 percent, and Mexico, Canada and the U.S. 1.36, 0.10 and 0.22 percent. The effect of NAFTA given world tariff changes is 1.17, −0.06-0.06−0.06 and 0.08 percent, with real wage gains of 1.63, 0.31 and 0.11 percent. Mexico gains less than in the first counterfactual because diversion is larger: its volume of trade effect with the rest of the world is −0.23-0.23−0.23 percent instead of −0.08-0.08−0.08.

  • Model comparison: the welfare effects for Mexico, Canada and the U.S. are 0.41, −0.08-0.08−0.08 and 0.05 percent in a one-sector model (one tradable and one non-tradable sector, median tariffs, θ=4.5\theta=4.5θ=4.5), 0.50, −0.03-0.03−0.03 and 0.03 percent in a multi-sector model without materials (γnj=1\gamma^j_n=1γnj​=1), and 0.66, −0.04-0.04−0.04 and 0.04 percent in a multi-sector model without I-O linkages (γnj,j=1−γnj\gamma^{j,j}_n=1-\gamma^j_nγnj,j​=1−γnj​). Import growth from NAFTA partners is 60.99, 5.98 and 17.34 percent in the first, 88.08, 9.95 and 26.91 in the second and 98.96, 10.14 and 30.70 in the third, against 118.28, 11.11 and 40.52 in the benchmark. The paper summarizes that welfare effects are on average 71, 62 and 50 percent lower, and trade effects 50, 26 and 18 percent lower, than in the benchmark.

  • Unilateral liberalization: if each member alone removed all its import tariffs, welfare would change by 0.54, −0.03-0.03−0.03 and −0.02-0.02−0.02 percent for Mexico, Canada and the U.S., which reflects the standard optimal tariff argument.

  • Caliendo, Lorenzo and Fernando Parro. 2015. “Estimates of the Trade and Welfare Effects of NAFTA.” The Review of Economic Studies, 82(1): 1–44.

This is the assumed utility function of the representative household in country nnn. The argument CnjC^j_nCnj​ is final consumption of the composite good of sector jjj, and the exponent αnj\alpha^j_nαnj​ is a preference weight that differs by country and sector. The weights sum to one, so utility is homogeneous of degree one in the consumption vector, and doubling all quantities doubles utility. This is what allows welfare to be written later as real income.

The Cobb-Douglas form buys constant expenditure shares. Maximizing u(Cn)u(C_n)u(Cn​) subject to the budget constraint ∑j=1JPnjCnj=In\sum_{j=1}^JP^j_nC^j_n=I_n∑j=1J​Pnj​Cnj​=In​ gives the first-order conditions αnju/Cnj=μPnj\alpha^j_nu/C^j_n=\mu P^j_nαnj​u/Cnj​=μPnj​ with multiplier μ\muμ, and summing them over jjj gives u=μInu=\mu I_nu=μIn​, so that

PnjCnj=αnjInP^j_nC^j_n=\alpha^j_nI_nPnj​Cnj​=αnj​In​

The household spends the fraction αnj\alpha^j_nαnj​ of income on sector jjj whatever the prices are. The elasticity of substitution across sectors is one, the own-price elasticity of demand is minus one, and all income elasticities are one. The form therefore rules out shifts of expenditure shares across sectors when tariffs change relative prices, and it rules out non-homothetic demand.

The equation is used three times in the note. As an illustration, if αnj=0.8\alpha^j_n=0.8αnj​=0.8 for the group of non-tradable sectors, 80 percent of final spending falls on goods whose prices change with tariffs only through their tradable inputs, which is why the input-output structure matters for welfare.

The Cobb-Douglas form implies that each input receives a constant share of cost, and by zero profits a constant share of revenue:

They also make the expenditure equation (11) and the labour market condition (14) linear in sectoral output. What the form rules out is any change in input shares when relative input prices change; a fall in the price of imported materials leaves the cost share of materials unchanged.

This is the technology of the producers of the composite intermediate good of sector jjj in country nnn. This equation defines the total trade cost that a sector jjj good faces when it is shipped from the exporter iii to the importer nnn. The first subscript is always the destination and the second the origin. The cost has two parts that multiply.

The iceberg cost dnij≥1d^j_{ni}\geq1dnij​≥1 is a real resource cost. To deliver one unit, dnijd^j_{ni}dnij​ units must be produced, and the difference is lost in transit. It includes transport, distance and non-tariff barriers, and it generates no income for anyone. The ad-valorem tariff τnij\tau^j_{ni}τnij​ is charged on the unit price of the good at the border, so the buyer pays τ~nij=1+τnij\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni}=1+\tau^j_{ni}τ~nij​=1+τnij​ dollars per dollar received by the seller. The tariff is a transfer and not a loss: it raises revenue RnR_nRn​ for the importer, which is rebated to households in equation (12). For domestic sales κnnj=1\kappa^j_{nn}=1κnnj​=1, because dnnj=1d^j_{nn}=1dnnj​=1 and no tariff is charged at home.

For the choice of supplier only the product matters, so both parts enter prices and trade shares in the same way, with the same elasticity:

ln⁡κnij=ln⁡τ~nij+ln⁡dnij,∂ln⁡πnij∂ln⁡τ~nij=∂ln⁡πnij∂ln⁡dnij=−θj(1−πnij)\ln\kappa^j_{ni}=\ln\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni}+\ln d^j_{ni},\qquad\frac{\partial\ln\pi^j_{ni}}{\partial\ln\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni}}=\frac{\partial\ln\pi^j_{ni}}{\partial\ln d^j_{ni}}=-\theta^j\left(1-\pi^j_{ni}\right)lnκnij​=lnτ~nij​+lndnij​,∂lnτ~nij​∂lnπnij​​=∂lndnij​∂lnπnij​​=−θj(1−πnij​)

holding input costs fixed, by equation (10). This equality is what allows the trade elasticity to be estimated from tariffs alone in equation (29), although iceberg costs are not observed. The two parts differ in the accounting. Tariffs must be divided out to go from expenditure to the value received by the exporter, which is why 1+τnij1+\tau^j_{ni}1+τnij​ appears in the denominators of equations (11) and (13). In a counterfactual only tariffs change, so κ^nij\hat{\kappa}^j_{ni}κ^nij​ is a ratio of tariff factors, equation (20). As a numerical example, dnij=1.2d^j_{ni}=1.2dnij​=1.2 and τnij=0.1\tau^j_{ni}=0.1τnij​=0.1 give κnij=1.32\kappa^j_{ni}=1.32κnij​=1.32. The triangle inequality stated after the equation rules out cheaper delivery through a third country.

The minimum is taken over all NNN countries including nnn itself, for which κnnj=1\kappa^j_{nn}=1κnnj​=1. Because efficiencies are random draws, a country with a high input cost or a high tariff still supplies the goods for which its draw is high enough. This is the extensive margin: a tariff cut changes the set of goods for which each country is the cheapest source. For a non-tradable sector the trade cost from every foreign country is infinite, only the term i=ni=ni=n can attain the minimum, and the price is cnj/znj(ωj)c^j_n/z^j_n(\omega^j)cnj​/znj​(ωj).

This is the assumed distribution of the efficiency znj(ωj)z^j_n(\omega^j)znj​(ωj) across the goods of sector jjj in country nnn; Fnj(z)F^j_n(z)Fnj​(z) is the probability that a draw is no larger than zzz. It is the Frechet (type II extreme value) distribution, with two parameters.

The location parameter λnj\lambda^j_nλnj​ shifts the whole distribution: a larger λnj\lambda^j_nλnj​ makes high draws more likely for every good, which is absolute advantage of country nnn in sector jjj. The shape parameter θj\theta^jθj controls dispersion and is common to all countries within a sector. Two moments make the roles clear:

A large θj\theta^jθj means that countries are similar good by good, and a small change in cost moves many goods from one supplier to another.

P^n=∏j=1J(P^nj)αnj,dln⁡Pn=∑j=1Jαnjdln⁡Pnj\hat{P}_n=\prod_{j=1}^J\left(\hat{P}^j_n\right)^{\alpha^j_n},\qquad d\ln P_n=\sum_{j=1}^J\alpha^j_nd\ln P^j_nP^n​=j=1∏J​(P^nj​)αnj​,dlnPn​=j=1∑J​αnj​dlnPnj​

The first form is used for the real wage in equation (21) and the second for the welfare formula in equation (22). The prices PnjP^j_nPnj​ are the same composite prices that firms pay for materials, because final goods and materials are the same composite good.

The expenditure share is derived in two parts: the probability that country iii is the cheapest source of a good, and the result that this probability is also the share of spending. Use the price distributions GnijG^j_{ni}Gnij​ and GnjG^j_nGnj​ and the statistic Φnj\Phi^j_nΦnj​ from the derivation of equation (8).

Step 1, the probability that iii offers the lowest price in nnn. Condition on the price ppp offered by iii and require all other offers to be higher:

Pr⁡(i is the cheapest source in n)=∫0∞∏h≠i[1−Gnhj(p)]dGnij(p)\Pr\left(i\text{ is the cheapest source in }n\right)=\int_0^\infty\prod_{h\neq i}\left[1-G^j_{nh}(p)\right]dG^j_{ni}(p)Pr(i is the cheapest source in n)=∫0∞​h=i∏​[1−Gnhj​(p)]dGnij​(p)

Step 2, insert the distributions. The density of GnijG^j_{ni}Gnij​ is λij(cijκnij)−θjθjpθj−1exp⁡{−λij(cijκnij)−θjpθj}\lambda^j_i(c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni})^{-\theta^j}\theta^jp^{\theta^j-1}\exp\{-\lambda^j_i(c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni})^{-\theta^j}p^{\theta^j}\}λij​(cij​κnij​)−θjθjpθj−1exp{−λij​(cij​κnij​)−θjpθj}, and the exponentials multiply to exp⁡{−Φnjpθj}\exp\{-\Phi^j_np^{\theta^j}\}exp{−Φnj​pθj}:

The last integral equals one because its integrand is the density of GnjG^j_nGnj​.

Step 3, the distribution of prices actually paid. Stopping the integral of Step 2 at a price pˉ\bar{p}pˉ​ gives the joint probability that iii is the cheapest source and that its price is below pˉ\bar{p}pˉ​:

λij(cijκnij)−θjΦnj[1−exp⁡{−Φnjpˉθj}]=Pr⁡(i is the cheapest source in n)×Gnj(pˉ)\frac{\lambda^j_i\left(c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni}\right)^{-\theta^j}}{\Phi^j_n}\left[1-\exp\left\{-\Phi^j_n\bar{p}^{\theta^j}\right\}\right]=\Pr\left(i\text{ is the cheapest source in }n\right)\times G^j_n(\bar{p})Φnj​λij​(cij​κnij​)−θj​[1−exp{−Φnj​pˉ​θj}]=Pr(i is the cheapest source in n)×Gnj​(pˉ​)

So the price of a good bought from iii has the distribution GnjG^j_nGnj​, the same for every source. A source with lower costs sells more goods, not cheaper goods on average.

Step 4, from goods to spending. Spending on a good depends only on its price, through the demand in equation (4). Since the distribution of prices is the same for every source, average spending per good is the same for every source, and the share of spending equals the share of goods:

πnij=XnijXnj=λij[cijκnij]−θj∑h=1Nλhj[chjκnhj]−θj\pi^j_{ni}=\frac{X^j_{ni}}{X^j_n}=\frac{\lambda^j_i\left[c^j_i\kappa^j_{ni}\right]^{-\theta^j}}{\sum_{h=1}^N\lambda^j_h\left[c^j_h\kappa^j_{nh}\right]^{-\theta^j}}πnij​=Xnj​Xnij​​=∑h=1N​λhj​[chj​κnhj​]−θjλij​[cij​κnij​]−θj​

In a non-tradable sector πnnj=1\pi^j_{nn}=1πnnj​=1.

The expenditure equation is the market-clearing condition for the composite good of sector jjj in country nnn, written in values. The composite good is used as material by the producers of every sector kkk in nnn and as final good by households:

Xnj=PnjQnj=∑k=1J∫Pnjmnj,k(ωk)dωk+PnjCnjX^j_n=P^j_nQ^j_n=\sum_{k=1}^J\int P^j_nm^{j,k}_n(\omega^k)d\omega^k+P^j_nC^j_nXnj​=Pnj​Qnj​=k=1∑J​∫Pnj​mnj,k​(ωk)dωk+Pnj​Cnj​

Step 1, materials. By the Cobb-Douglas technology of equation (2), a producer of sector kkk spends the fraction γnj,k\gamma^{j,k}_nγnj,k​ of its cost on materials from sector jjj, and with zero profits cost equals revenue. Integrating over the goods of sector kkk:

∫Pnjmnj,k(ωk)dωk=γnj,k×(revenue of sector k producers in n)\int P^j_nm^{j,k}_n(\omega^k)d\omega^k=\gamma^{j,k}_n\times\left(\text{revenue of sector }k\text{ producers in }n\right)∫Pnj​mnj,k​(ωk)dωk=γnj,k​×(revenue of sector k producers in n)

Step 2, revenue. Buyers in country iii spend XikπinkX^k_i\pi^k_{in}Xik​πink​ on sector kkk goods from nnn, by the definition of the share in equation (10). This amount includes the tariff collected by iii, so the producers in nnn receive it divided by 1+τink1+\tau^k_{in}1+τink​. Summing over all destinations, the home market included:

revenue of sector k producers in n=∑i=1NXikπink1+τink\text{revenue of sector }k\text{ producers in }n=\sum_{i=1}^NX^k_i\frac{\pi^k_{in}}{1+\tau^k_{in}}revenue of sector k producers in n=i=1∑N​Xik​1+τink​πink​​

Iceberg costs need no correction: the units lost in transit are produced and paid for with labour and materials, so they are part of the cost that this revenue covers.

Step 3, final demand. By the Cobb-Douglas demand derived from equation (1), PnjCnj=αnjInP^j_nC^j_n=\alpha^j_nI_nPnj​Cnj​=αnj​In​.

Step 4, add the parts:

Xnj=∑k=1Jγnj,k∑i=1NXikπink1+τink+αnjInX^j_n=\sum_{k=1}^J\gamma^{j,k}_n\sum_{i=1}^NX^k_i\frac{\pi^k_{in}}{1+\tau^k_{in}}+\alpha^j_nI_nXnj​=k=1∑J​γnj,k​i=1∑N​Xik​1+τink​πink​​+αnj​In​

Note the order of the superscripts: γnj,k\gamma^{j,k}_nγnj,k​ is the share of sector jjj in the cost of sector kkk, so the equation sums over the using sectors kkk. Given trade shares, tariffs and income, the equations for all (n,j)(n,j)(n,j) form a linear system in the expenditures, which is how they are solved in equation (26). The system links countries, because the output of sector kkk in nnn depends on expenditure in every destination iii, and it links sectors through the input-output shares.

The first part is the budget constraint of the household sector of country nnn, and the second is the definition of tariff revenue. The variable InI_nIn​ is final absorption: the value of final goods that households buy. It has three sources.

Labour income wnLnw_nL_nwn​Ln​ is the only factor income, because there are no profits. Tariff revenue RnR_nRn​ is rebated to households as a lump sum. The trade deficit DnD_nDn​ is a transfer from the rest of the world: a country with Dn>0D_n>0Dn​>0 spends more than it earns. The deficit is exogenous and the model does not explain it; it is in the equation so that the base year matches the data. Deficits sum to zero across countries.

In the revenue term, Mnij=Xnjπnij/(1+τnij)M^j_{ni}=X^j_n\pi^j_{ni}/(1+\tau^j_{ni})Mnij​=Xnj​πnij​/(1+τnij​) is the value of imports before the tariff, which is the tax base of an ad-valorem tariff. The sum may include i=ni=ni=n, since τnnj=0\tau^j_{nn}=0τnnj​=0. Revenue can be written with expenditures and shares only, which is the form used in equations (20) and (26):

Rn=∑j=1J∑i=1Nτnij1+τnijπnijXnj=∑j=1JXnj(1−∑i=1Nπnij1+τnij)R_n=\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{\tau^j_{ni}}{1+\tau^j_{ni}}\pi^j_{ni}X^j_n=\sum_{j=1}^JX^j_n\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{\pi^j_{ni}}{1+\tau^j_{ni}}\right)Rn​=j=1∑J​i=1∑N​1+τnij​τnij​​πnij​Xnj​=j=1∑J​Xnj​(1−i=1∑N​1+τnij​πnij​​)

The second equality uses τ/(1+τ)=1−1/(1+τ)\tau/(1+\tau)=1-1/(1+\tau)τ/(1+τ)=1−1/(1+τ) and the fact that the shares sum to one over iii.

Revenue is endogenous. It depends on expenditures XnjX^j_nXnj​, which depend on InI_nIn​ through equation (11), so income and expenditure are determined together. The rebate is the reason why the real wage of equation (21) is not a measure of welfare: a tariff cut lowers prices but also changes RnR_nRn​. In the welfare formula (22) the mechanical loss of revenue from a lower tariff rate cancels exactly against the mechanical fall in consumer prices, and only the changes in the tax base remain, as the volume of trade term. As an example, a 10 percent tariff on imports worth 50 before the tariff yields revenue of 5, and buyers spend 55.

The trade balance condition is the definition of the aggregate deficit written with expenditures and shares. Start from the definitions given after equation (12). The aggregate deficit is the sum of sectoral deficits, and each sectoral deficit is imports minus exports, both valued before tariffs:

Dn=∑j=1JDnj=∑j=1J∑i=1NMnij−∑j=1J∑i=1NEnijD_n=\sum_{j=1}^JD^j_n=\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^NM^j_{ni}-\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^NE^j_{ni}Dn​=j=1∑J​Dnj​=j=1∑J​i=1∑N​Mnij​−j=1∑J​i=1∑N​Enij​

Step 1, substitute imports. Buyers in nnn spend XnjπnijX^j_n\pi^j_{ni}Xnj​πnij​ on sector jjj goods from iii, of which the exporter receives

Mnij=Xnjπnij1+τnijM^j_{ni}=X^j_n\frac{\pi^j_{ni}}{1+\tau^j_{ni}}Mnij​=Xnj​1+τnij​πnij​​

Step 2, substitute exports. The exports of nnn to iii are the imports of iii from nnn:

Enij=Minj=Xijπinj1+τinjE^j_{ni}=M^j_{in}=X^j_i\frac{\pi^j_{in}}{1+\tau^j_{in}}Enij​=Minj​=Xij​1+τinj​πinj​​

Step 3, rearrange the definition of the deficit with imports on the left and exports on the right:

∑j=1J∑i=1NXnjπnij1+τnij−Dn=∑j=1J∑i=1NXijπinj1+τinj\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^NX^j_n\frac{\pi^j_{ni}}{1+\tau^j_{ni}}-D_n=\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^NX^j_i\frac{\pi^j_{in}}{1+\tau^j_{in}}j=1∑J​i=1∑N​Xnj​1+τnij​πnij​​−Dn​=j=1∑J​i=1∑N​Xij​1+τinj​πinj​​

which is the target. Both sums include the term i=ni=ni=n, which is domestic sales XnjπnnjX^j_n\pi^j_{nn}Xnj​πnnj​ on each side and cancels; it is kept so that the left-hand side is total expenditure net of tariff payments and the right-hand side is total gross output. For the same reason non-tradable sectors, where πnnj=1\pi^j_{nn}=1πnnj​=1, appear on both sides and cancel.

The condition is an equilibrium restriction because DnD_nDn​ is treated as an exogenous number while both sides depend on wages. Given the linear system of equation (11), it provides one equation per country to determine the NNN wages. Summing the condition over all countries gives ∑nDn=0\sum_nD_n=0∑n​Dn​=0 identically, so only N−1N-1N−1 of the conditions are independent, and one wage or world income must be normalized.

Labour market clearing follows from the expenditure equation (11), the income definition (12) and the trade balance (13). To shorten the notation in this derivation write the gross output of sector kkk in country nnn as

∑j=1JXnj=∑k=1J(1−γnk)Ynk+wnLn+∑j=1JXnj−∑j=1J∑i=1NXnjπnij1+τnij+Dn\sum_{j=1}^JX^j_n=\sum_{k=1}^J\left(1-\gamma^k_n\right)Y^k_n+w_nL_n+\sum_{j=1}^JX^j_n-\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^NX^j_n\frac{\pi^j_{ni}}{1+\tau^j_{ni}}+D_nj=1∑J​Xnj​=k=1∑J​(1−γnk​)Ynk​+wn​Ln​+j=1∑J​Xnj​−j=1∑J​i=1∑N​Xnj​1+τnij​πnij​​+Dn​

The right-hand side is the labour demand of all sectors in values: each sector pays the fraction γnj\gamma^j_nγnj​ of its revenue to labour, by equation (2). This is equation (3) in relative changes. Write equation (3) under the counterfactual tariffs τ′\tau'τ′ and under the baseline tariffs τ\tauτ. With the notation x^=x′/x\hat{x}=x'/xx^=x′/x this is

The result is exact for changes of any size, not a first-order approximation, because equation (3) is multiplicative. No level of wages or prices is needed, only the shares. This is the price index (8) in relative changes. Raise equation (8) to the power −θj-\theta^j−θj under both tariff structures. Technologies λij\lambda^j_iλij​, the constant AjA^jAj and the parameter θj\theta^jθj do not change:

(Pnj′)−θj=(Aj)−θj∑i=1Nλij(cij′κnij′)−θj,(Pnj)−θj=(Aj)−θj∑h=1Nλhj(chjκnhj)−θj\left(P^{j'}_n\right)^{-\theta^j}=\left(A^j\right)^{-\theta^j}\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda^j_i\left(c^{j'}_i\kappa^{j'}_{ni}\right)^{-\theta^j},\qquad\left(P^j_n\right)^{-\theta^j}=\left(A^j\right)^{-\theta^j}\sum_{h=1}^N\lambda^j_h\left(c^j_h\kappa^j_{nh}\right)^{-\theta^j}(Pnj′​)−θj=(Aj)−θji=1∑N​λij​(cij′​κnij′​)−θj,(Pnj​)−θj=(Aj)−θjh=1∑N​λhj​(chj​κnhj​)−θj

(P^nj)−θj=∑i=1Nπnij(κ^nijc^ij)−θj\left(\hat{P}^j_n\right)^{-\theta^j}=\sum_{i=1}^N\pi^j_{ni}\left(\hat{\kappa}^j_{ni}\hat{c}^j_i\right)^{-\theta^j}(P^nj​)−θj=i=1∑N​πnij​(κ^nij​c^ij​)−θj

This is the central step of the hat algebra. The printed version is the special case in which the exogenous deficit is held at its baseline value when tariffs change:

The distinction matters in the application. The paper's benchmark first removes all deficits by solving the model with Dn′=0D'_n=0Dn′​=0 and unchanged tariffs, and then uses that economy as the base, so that the deficit is zero before and after. Its alternative holds deficits fixed as a share of world GDP, in which case Dn′D'_nDn′​ differs from DnD_nDn​ in nominal terms. The solution system (26) is written with the same Dn′D'_nDn′​.

A deficit that is fixed in nominal terms and different from zero also makes the choice of numeraire matter, because the equilibrium conditions are then not homogeneous of degree zero in wages: scaling all wage changes changes the real size of the transfer. With Dn′=0D'_n=0Dn′​=0 the system is homogeneous, and wages are determined up to a normalization. Given the shares from equation (17) and the expenditures from equation (18), the condition is one equation per country in the wage changes w^n\hat{w}_nw^n​.

The two expressions define the inputs of equations (16) to (19) in terms of the policy change and of baseline data.

which is the target, with the three terms labelled final goods, intermediate goods and sectoral linkages. The formula is exact for changes of any size and requires γnj>0\gamma^j_n>0γnj​>0 in every sector with αnj>0\alpha^j_n>0αnj​>0.

The special cases follow directly. If γnj=1\gamma^j_n=1γnj​=1 for all jjj, then all γnk,j\gamma^{k,j}_nγnk,j​ are zero, the second and third terms vanish, and only the first remains. This defines the bilateral terms of trade measure between country nnn and partner iii. It is the part of the first term of equation (22) that involves partner iii, before division by income.

The measure is positive when the prices of what nnn sells to iii rise relative to the prices of what it buys from iii, with trade values as weights.

The notation needs care. Despite the symbol dln⁡d\lndln, the right-hand side is a sum of values times log changes and is measured in units of currency, not in logs. It becomes a contribution to the percentage change in welfare only after division by InI_nIn​:

which is the terms of trade effect of equation (22). For i=ni=ni=n the measure is zero, because Ennj=MnnjE^j_{nn}=M^j_{nn}Ennj​=Mnnj​ and the cost change is the same. The sectoral measure dln⁡totnjd\ln tot^j_ndlntotnj​ fixes jjj and sums over partners, and both breakdowns add up to the same total.

The sign cannot be determined in general. A tariff cut by nnn lowers the cost of materials in nnn and hence cnjc^j_ncnj​, which worsens the terms of trade, while higher demand for the labour of nnn raises the wage and works in the other direction. In the paper's results the first force dominates for Mexico, whose terms of trade with its NAFTA partners deteriorate. Bilateral measures need not be equal and opposite across the two partners, since each is weighted by the country's own trade values; world prices are measured relative to a numeraire.

This defines the bilateral volume of trade measure between country nnn and partner iii, the part of the second term of equation (22) that involves partner iii.

Each sector contributes the product of two factors. The first, τnijMnij\tau^j_{ni}M^j_{ni}τnij​Mnij​, is the tariff revenue that nnn collects on sector jjj imports from iii in the baseline. The second, dln⁡Mnij−dln⁡cijd\ln M^j_{ni}-d\ln c^j_idlnMnij​−dlncij​, is the change in the value of imports before tariffs minus the change in their pre-tariff price, that is, the proportional change in the quantity imported. The product is the change in revenue caused by the change in quantity alone at the initial tariff rate.

The reason why this is a welfare effect is the wedge that a tariff creates. Buyers in nnn value the marginal imported unit at the tariff-inclusive price, while the country as a whole pays only the pre-tariff price, because the difference returns to households as revenue. One more unit imported across a tariff therefore yields a gain equal to the tariff:

(1+τnij)cijdnijzij(ωj)⏟value to the buyer−cijdnijzij(ωj)⏟cost to the country=τnijcijdnijzij(ωj)\underbrace{\left(1+\tau^j_{ni}\right)\frac{c^j_id^j_{ni}}{z^j_i(\omega^j)}}_{\text{value to the buyer}}-\underbrace{\frac{c^j_id^j_{ni}}{z^j_i(\omega^j)}}_{\text{cost to the country}}=\tau^j_{ni}\frac{c^j_id^j_{ni}}{z^j_i(\omega^j)}value to the buyer(1+τnij​)zij​(ωj)cij​dnij​​​​−cost to the countryzij​(ωj)cij​dnij​​​​=τnij​zij​(ωj)cij​dnij​​

The initial tariff is the weight, not the change in the tariff. Trade created with a partner whose goods carry a positive tariff raises welfare. Trade diverted away from a non-member whose goods still pay a tariff lowers it, because revenue on those imports is lost. If the initial tariff on a flow is zero, a change in that flow has no first-order welfare effect. This is the classical distinction between trade creation and trade diversion, and summing the measure over NAFTA partners and over the rest of the world separates the two in the results.

As for equation (23), the symbol dln⁡d\lndln is only a label: the right-hand side is in units of currency and is divided by InI_nIn​ in equation (22). The term for i=ni=ni=n is zero since τnnj=0\tau^j_{nn}=0τnnj​=0. As an illustration, if imports from iii in a sector are 100 before tariffs, the tariff is 10 percent and the quantity imported rises by 20 percent, the contribution is 0.1×100×0.2=20.1\times100\times0.2=20.1×100×0.2=2 units of currency.

XnhjXhijXinj=(ShjSijSnj)(BnjBhjBij)(κnhjκhijκinj)−θjX^j_{nh}X^j_{hi}X^j_{in}=\left(S^j_hS^j_iS^j_n\right)\left(B^j_nB^j_hB^j_i\right)\left(\kappa^j_{nh}\kappa^j_{hi}\kappa^j_{in}\right)^{-\theta^j}Xnhj​Xhij​Xinj​=(Shj​Sij​Snj​)(Bnj​Bhj​Bij​)(κnhj​κhij​κinj​)−θj

Step 3, divide. In each product every country appears exactly once as exporter and exactly once as importer, so the two brackets with SSS and BBB are identical in numerator and denominator and cancel:

XnijXihjXhnjXnhjXhijXinj=(κnijκihjκhnjκnhjκhijκinj)−θj\frac{X^j_{ni}X^j_{ih}X^j_{hn}}{X^j_{nh}X^j_{hi}X^j_{in}}=\left(\frac{\kappa^j_{ni}\kappa^j_{ih}\kappa^j_{hn}}{\kappa^j_{nh}\kappa^j_{hi}\kappa^j_{in}}\right)^{-\theta^j}Xnhj​Xhij​Xinj​Xnij​Xihj​Xhnj​​=(κnhj​κhij​κinj​κnij​κihj​κhnj​​)−θj

Step 4, pair each trade cost with the cost of the reverse flow:

XnijXihjXhnjXnhjXhijXinj=(κnijκinjκihjκhijκhnjκnhj)−θj\frac{X^j_{ni}X^j_{ih}X^j_{hn}}{X^j_{nh}X^j_{hi}X^j_{in}}=\left(\frac{\kappa^j_{ni}}{\kappa^j_{in}}\frac{\kappa^j_{ih}}{\kappa^j_{hi}}\frac{\kappa^j_{hn}}{\kappa^j_{nh}}\right)^{-\theta^j}Xnhj​Xhij​Xinj​Xnij​Xihj​Xhnj​​=(κinj​κnij​​κhij​κihj​​κnhj​κhnj​​)−θj

which is the target. Everything that is specific to a country has gone: technologies, input costs, total expenditures and the price terms Φnj\Phi^j_nΦnj​, none of which is observed directly. What remains is a product of three ratios, each comparing the cost of trade in one direction with the cost in the reverse direction for one pair. If trade costs were symmetric for every pair, the right-hand side would equal one, so the ratio measures asymmetries in trade flows that are due to asymmetries in trade costs.

The cancellation uses only the multiplicative structure exporter term times importer term times bilateral term, which is why the method is valid in any model with such a gravity equation. Domestic flows XnnjX^j_{nn}Xnnj​ are not used, unlike in the Head and Ries ratio, which is helpful because domestic sales require production data. Three is the smallest number of countries for which the ratio is informative: with two countries the same construction gives XnijXinj/(XinjXnij)=1X^j_{ni}X^j_{in}/(X^j_{in}X^j_{ni})=1Xnij​Xinj​/(Xinj​Xnij​)=1.

This is an assumption about the structure of trade costs, used to turn the triple ratio (27) into a regression. The first equality is the log of equation (5): the total cost is the tariff factor times the iceberg cost. The second equality is the assumption that the unobserved log iceberg cost has four components.

The component νnij\nu^j_{ni}νnij​ is symmetric, νnij=νinj\nu^j_{ni}=\nu^j_{in}νnij​=νinj​. It stands for everything that affects trade between two countries equally in both directions, such as distance, a common language, a common border or membership of the same free trade area. The component μnj\mu^j_nμnj​ is common to all imports of country nnn in sector jjj whatever their origin, for example a non-tariff barrier that nnn applies to all partners. The component δij\delta^j_iδij​ is common to all exports of country iii in sector jjj whatever their destination, for example an export cost. The last component εnij\varepsilon^j_{ni}εnij​ is an idiosyncratic deviation that differs by direction, and it is assumed to be orthogonal to tariffs.

The specification is more general than the usual symmetry assumption, because iceberg costs may differ by direction through the importer and exporter effects and through the error:

ln⁡dnij−ln⁡dinj=(μnj−μij)+(δij−δnj)+(εnij−εinj)\ln d^j_{ni}-\ln d^j_{in}=\left(\mu^j_n-\mu^j_i\right)+\left(\delta^j_i-\delta^j_n\right)+\left(\varepsilon^j_{ni}-\varepsilon^j_{in}\right)lndnij​−lndinj​=(μnj​−μij​)+(δij​−δnj​)+(εnij​−εinj​)

The symmetric part has dropped out of this difference, and the importer and exporter effects enter as differences between the two countries. These are the terms that telescope to zero around a triangle of three countries, which gives equation (29).

What the specification rules out is a systematic directional component of trade costs that is specific to a pair and correlated with tariffs. An example would be a non-tariff barrier that nnn applies only to imports from iii and that is used as a substitute for a low tariff on iii. Such a barrier would be part of εnij\varepsilon^j_{ni}εnij​ and would bias the estimate. No functional form is imposed on the symmetric part, so distance and the other gravity variables need not be measured. Tariffs enter with a unit coefficient in ln⁡κnij\ln\kappa^j_{ni}lnκnij​, which means that the trade elasticity is the same for tariffs and for other trade costs, by equation (10).

Take logs of the triple ratio (27). The denominator in the target lists the same three flows as in equation (27) in a different order:

ln⁡(XnijXihjXhnjXinjXhijXnhj)=−θj[(ln⁡κnij−ln⁡κinj)+(ln⁡κihj−ln⁡κhij)+(ln⁡κhnj−ln⁡κnhj)]\ln\left(\frac{X^j_{ni}X^j_{ih}X^j_{hn}}{X^j_{in}X^j_{hi}X^j_{nh}}\right)=-\theta^j\left[\left(\ln\kappa^j_{ni}-\ln\kappa^j_{in}\right)+\left(\ln\kappa^j_{ih}-\ln\kappa^j_{hi}\right)+\left(\ln\kappa^j_{hn}-\ln\kappa^j_{nh}\right)\right]ln(Xinj​Xhij​Xnhj​Xnij​Xihj​Xhnj​​)=−θj[(lnκnij​−lnκinj​)+(lnκihj​−lnκhij​)+(lnκhnj​−lnκnhj​)]

Step 1, one pair. Apply equation (28) to both directions of the pair nnn and iii and subtract. The symmetric term cancels because νnij=νinj\nu^j_{ni}=\nu^j_{in}νnij​=νinj​:

ln⁡κnij−ln⁡κinj=ln⁡τ~nijτ~inj+(μnj−μij)+(δij−δnj)+(εnij−εinj)\ln\kappa^j_{ni}-\ln\kappa^j_{in}=\ln\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{in}}+\left(\mu^j_n-\mu^j_i\right)+\left(\delta^j_i-\delta^j_n\right)+\left(\varepsilon^j_{ni}-\varepsilon^j_{in}\right)lnκnij​−lnκinj​=lnτ~inj​τ~nij​​+(μnj​−μij​)+(δij​−δnj​)+(εnij​−εinj​)

Step 2, the other two pairs, by the same argument:

ln⁡κihj−ln⁡κhij=ln⁡τ~ihjτ~hij+(μij−μhj)+(δhj−δij)+(εihj−εhij)ln⁡κhnj−ln⁡κnhj=ln⁡τ~hnjτ~nhj+(μhj−μnj)+(δnj−δhj)+(εhnj−εnhj)\begin{aligned} \ln\kappa^j_{ih}-\ln\kappa^j_{hi}&=\ln\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{ih}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{hi}}+\left(\mu^j_i-\mu^j_h\right)+\left(\delta^j_h-\delta^j_i\right)+\left(\varepsilon^j_{ih}-\varepsilon^j_{hi}\right)\\ \ln\kappa^j_{hn}-\ln\kappa^j_{nh}&=\ln\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{hn}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{nh}}+\left(\mu^j_h-\mu^j_n\right)+\left(\delta^j_n-\delta^j_h\right)+\left(\varepsilon^j_{hn}-\varepsilon^j_{nh}\right) \end{aligned}lnκihj​−lnκhij​lnκhnj​−lnκnhj​​=lnτ~hij​τ~ihj​​+(μij​−μhj​)+(δhj​−δij​)+(εihj​−εhij​)=lnτ~nhj​τ~hnj​​+(μhj​−μnj​)+(δnj​−δhj​)+(εhnj​−εnhj​)​

Step 3, add the three lines. The importer effects and the exporter effects telescope around the triangle:

(μnj−μij)+(μij−μhj)+(μhj−μnj)=0,(δij−δnj)+(δhj−δij)+(δnj−δhj)=0\left(\mu^j_n-\mu^j_i\right)+\left(\mu^j_i-\mu^j_h\right)+\left(\mu^j_h-\mu^j_n\right)=0,\qquad\left(\delta^j_i-\delta^j_n\right)+\left(\delta^j_h-\delta^j_i\right)+\left(\delta^j_n-\delta^j_h\right)=0(μnj​−μij​)+(μij​−μhj​)+(μhj​−μnj​)=0,(δij​−δnj​)+(δhj​−δij​)+(δnj​−δhj​)=0

Each country is an importer in one flow of the numerator and in one flow of the denominator, and the same holds for its role as exporter, so each fixed effect enters once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign.

Step 4, collect what remains:

ln⁡(XnijXihjXhnjXinjXhijXnhj)=−θjln⁡(τ~nijτ~injτ~ihjτ~hijτ~hnjτ~nhj)+θj(εinj−εnij+εhij−εihj+εnhj−εhnj)\ln\left(\frac{X^j_{ni}X^j_{ih}X^j_{hn}}{X^j_{in}X^j_{hi}X^j_{nh}}\right)=-\theta^j\ln\left(\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{ni}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{in}}\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{ih}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{hi}}\frac{\tilde{\tau}^j_{hn}}{\tilde{\tau}^j_{nh}}\right)+\theta^j\left(\varepsilon^j_{in}-\varepsilon^j_{ni}+\varepsilon^j_{hi}-\varepsilon^j_{ih}+\varepsilon^j_{nh}-\varepsilon^j_{hn}\right)ln(Xinj​Xhij​Xnhj​Xnij​Xihj​Xhnj​​)=−θjln(τ~inj​τ~nij​​τ~hij​τ~ihj​​τ~nhj​τ~hnj​​)+θj(εinj​−εnij​+εhij​−εihj​+εnhj​−εhnj​)

This is the target with the error term

ε~j=θj(εinj−εnij+εhij−εihj+εnhj−εhnj)\tilde{\varepsilon}^j=\theta^j\left(\varepsilon^j_{in}-\varepsilon^j_{ni}+\varepsilon^j_{hi}-\varepsilon^j_{ih}+\varepsilon^j_{nh}-\varepsilon^j_{hn}\right)ε~j=θj(εinj​−εnij​+εhij​−εihj​+εnhj​−εhnj​)

The note, following the paper, defines ε~j\tilde{\varepsilon}^jε~j as the bracket alone, without the factor θj\theta^jθj. The algebra gives the factor. The omission does not affect the regression, since θj\theta^jθj is a constant within a sector and the error is orthogonal to tariffs with or without it; it only rescales the error.

The equation is a regression without a constant of the log triple ratio of trade flows on the log triple ratio of tariff factors, sector by sector, and the coefficient is minus the trade elasticity. Identification comes from asymmetries: if tariffs were the same in both directions for every pair, the regressor would be zero and θj\theta^jθj would not be identified. The estimator needs no data on prices, distance, production or domestic sales, and no assumption that trade costs are symmetric. It does require that the directional deviations in trade costs are not correlated with directional differences in tariffs. Each observation is a triple of countries, and the six flows of a triple must all be positive for the logarithm to exist, which is why zeros are dropped.
